answer.label: Written by

answer.sourceLine: It is a genuine line from The Imitation of Christ, Book I, chapter 21 (“Of compunction of heart”), the devotional book Thomas à Kempis composed in Latin around 1418–1427. This exact English phrasing is Rev. William Benham’s translation of the Latin “Certa viriliter: consuetudo consuetudine vincitur” — the thought is à Kempis’s, the Victorian diction is Benham’s.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: The Imitation of Christ (De Imitatione Christi)
Book I, chapter 21 — “Of compunction of heart”
Rev. William Benham (1831–1910); his English version was in print by 1874 (Macmillan) and reissued in an illustrated edition by J. C. Nimmo, London, 1886

source.excerpt: Happy is he who can cast away every cause of distraction and bring himself to the one purpose of holy compunction. Happy is he who putteth away from him whatsoever may stain or burden his conscience. Strive manfully; custom is overcome by custom. If thou knowest how to let men alone, they will gladly let thee alone to do thine own works.
trail: The Latin original sits in Caput 21, De compunctione cordis. The Latin text of Book I at The Latin Library ↗ punctuates it as two sentences — “Certa viriliter. Consuetudo consuetudine vincitur” — while a second Latin edition of the same chapter, with its surrounding sentences intact, prints “Certa viriliter: consuetudo consuetudine vincitur.” The pointing is editorial; the words are identical.

The familiar English — “Strive manfully; custom is overcome by custom” — is Rev. William Benham’s wording, printed in Book I, Chapter XXI (“Of compunction of heart”) of the Project Gutenberg edition of his translation ↗.

Other translators render the same Latin quite differently — one widely circulated English version of Book 1, chapter 21 reads “Fight like a man. Habit is overcome by habit” (Catholic Archive ↗). The sentence you know depends on which translator you happened to read.
Benham’s version had a long print run: the Online Books Page ↗ lists it under Macmillan (1874), C. T. Dillingham (1884), J. C. Nimmo (1886), G. Routledge & Sons (1905) and P. F. Collier (1909).
source.excerptNote: Benham’s English. The Latin of the same passage, in The Latin Library’s text, reads: “Felix qui abjicere potest omne impedimentum distractionis, et ad unionem se redigere sanctæ compunctionis. Felix qui a se abdicat quidquid suam conscientiam maculare potest, vel gravare. Certa viriliter. Consuetudo consuetudine vincitur.” Punctuation is editorial and varies between editions — other Latin printings run the last two clauses together as “Certa viriliter: consuetudo consuetudine vincitur,” the form quoted elsewhere on this page.

source.rightsNote: The Latin original was composed c. 1418–1427 and has been in the public domain for centuries. The English wording quoted here is William Benham’s translation, in print by 1874 and reissued through 1909 — all well before the 1931 U.S. cutoff, so this rendering is public domain too. A modern translation of the same Latin sentence would not be: post-1930 English versions of the Imitation are separately copyrightable works.

author.name: Thomas à Kempis
author.heading: Who was Thomas à Kempis?
author.metaLine: c. 1380 – 1 May 1471 · German-Dutch canon regular & devotional writer
author.bio: Thomas à Kempis was a German-Dutch canon regular of the Augustinians in the Congregation of Windesheim, shaped by the Modern Devotion movement. He entered the monastery of Mount Saint Agnes near Zwolle in 1406 and became its sub-prior in 1429, spending a long life copying manuscripts and instructing novices. He is remembered almost entirely for one book, The Imitation of Christ, written c. 1418–1427 — a work Thomas More reportedly called one of the three everybody ought to own.

misattribution.heading: What people get wrong
misattribution.intro: The line itself is genuine, but two things around it are routinely garbled — who wrote the book it comes from, and whose English you are actually quoting.

items.who: Giovanni Gersen, abbot of Saint Etienne de Verceil
items.why: The Imitation of Christ circulated anonymously, and Italian Benedictines pressed a claim for Gersen, placing the work around 1250 — roughly two centuries before à Kempis. Wikipedia’s account of the authorship controversy ↗ notes that modern scholars nonetheless accept à Kempis, on the strength of contemporary manuscripts bearing his name.

items.who: Jean Gerson, chancellor of the University of Paris
items.why: French scholars advanced Gerson as the author; other names floated over the centuries included Bonaventure, Bernard of Clairvaux, Henri Kalkar and Ludolph of Saxony, and some critics argued the book was an impersonal compilation of medieval mystics rather than one man’s work (The Imitation of Christ ↗).

“Strive manfully; custom is overcome by custom” is Benham’s Victorian English, not a sentence à Kempis wrote. He wrote Latin: “Certa viriliter: consuetudo consuetudine vincitur.” Quote Investigator makes the same point about another line from this book, tracking how far apart its translators land ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Thomas à Kempis wrote the thought, in Latin, in Book I, chapter 21 of The Imitation of Christ; the sentence in English is William Benham’s translation ↗. Both are true at once, and quoting the second as à Kempis’s exact words is the small, common slip.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Chapter 21 of Book I is about compunctio cordis — the sting of conscience that the Modern Devotion movement treated as the engine of self-reform. À Kempis was writing for novices at Mount Saint Agnes near Zwolle, where he had entered in 1406 and served as sub-prior from 1429, and the chapter reads less like a sermon than like instructions for men trying to change how they actually behave day to day.

That is what gives the line its unsentimental force. He does not tell the reader to resolve harder or feel worse; he tells him that a habit is displaced by another habit, and that the work is a fight. It is practical monastic psychology, and it is the same principle every modern habit-formation book restates.
detailsBody: The book was written as four booklets and spread with extraordinary speed for the era: roughly 750 manuscripts survived by 1471, copied out by hand across monastic houses, and the first printed edition appeared in Augsburg around 1471–72.

An autograph manuscript in à Kempis’s own hand, dated 1441, is preserved at the Bibliothèque Royale in Brussels (MS 5855-61) — part of the evidence that eventually settled the long authorship quarrel in his favour.
context.pull: A habit is not argued away. It is replaced.

sourcesVerified.claim: The exact wording "Strive manfully; custom is overcome by custom" appears in Book I, Chapter XXI ("Of compunction of heart") of The Imitation of Christ in Rev. William Benham's translation, in the passage beginning "Happy is he who can cast away every cause of distraction..."

The Latin of the same passage, in Cap. 21 "De compunctione cordis" of Book I, reads "Felix qui abjicere potest omne impedimentum distractionis, et ad unionem se redigere sanctae compunctionis. Felix qui a se abdicat quidquid suam conscientiam maculare potest, vel gravare. Certa viriliter. Consuetudo consuetudine vincitur."

A second Latin edition confirms Caput 21 contains "Certa viriliter: consuetudo consuetudine vincitur", preceded by "Felix! qui abjicere potest omne impedimentum distractionis, et ad unionem se redigere sancte compunctionis." and "Felix! qui a se abdicat, quicquid conscientiam suam maculare potest vel gravare." — the same words as The Latin Library's text, differently pointed.

Another English translation of Book 1, chapter 21 renders the same Latin as "Fight like a man. Habit is overcome by habit. If you leave men alone, they will leave you alone to do what you have to do."

William Benham's translation, 'The imitation of Christ: four books', was published by J. C. Nimmo in London in 1886, with Thomas a Kempis (1380-1471) as author and William Benham (1831-1910) as translator.
Benham's Imitation translation was printed by Macmillan in 1874, C. T. Dillingham in 1884, J. C. Nimmo in 1886, G. Routledge & Sons in 1905, and P. F. Collier in 1909.

The Imitation of Christ was composed in Medieval Latin c. 1418-1427, published anonymously, and was claimed for Giovanni Gersen (abbot of Saint Etienne de Verceil, c. 1250) by Italian Benedictines and for Jean Gerson by French scholars, with Bonaventure, Bernard of Clairvaux, Henri Kalkar and Ludolph of Saxony also proposed; modern scholars accept Thomas a Kempis. Roughly 750 manuscripts survived by 1471 and the first printed edition appeared in Augsburg c. 1471-72.

Thomas a Kempis was born c. 1380 and died 1 May 1471; he was a German-Dutch canon regular of the Augustinians in the Congregation of Windesheim, entered Mount Saint Agnes near Zwolle in 1406, served as sub-prior from 1429, and his 1441 autograph manuscript of the Imitation is at the Bibliotheque Royale in Brussels. Thomas More reportedly called it one of three books everybody ought to own. (The article gives the shelfmark as "MS 5455-61"; the scholarly literature has 5855-61, and this page follows the latter.)

The 1441 Thomas a Kempis autograph codex in Brussels carries the shelfmark Bruxellensis 5855-61: L. M. J. Delaisse's 1956 diplomatic edition is titled "Le manuscrit autographe de Thomas a Kempis et 'l'Imitation de Jesus-Christ'. Examen archeologique et edition diplomatique du Bruxellensis 5855-61".
